problem: Learning-based navigation foundation models fail outside their training distribution, and VLM-based navigation methods rarely ground their reasoning in the scene. Grounded variants reduce the VLM's answer to one fixed cue (a rule set or a trajectory pick), and slow VLM answers lag behind the dynamic scene.
motivation: A robot in diverse, dynamic environments must understand a complex scene (pedestrians to yield to, gaps to thread, terrain to avoid) and turn that understanding into stable motion. Current designs leave the VLM's semantics ungrounded or misaligned with action, and VLM latency of seconds makes them stale. A compact, grounded representation that bears directly on action, and stays aligned with the live scene, is missing.
key_idea: Decompose the scene with a VLM into four judgments (terrain traversability, collision risk, heading preference, passable gaps), ground them with vision foundation models into one Actionable Cost map that both conditions trajectory decoders and selects among their candidates, built on both a pivot frame and the current frame.
insight: Each map component adds a judgment the others cannot express: adding M^C, M^H and M^P step by step raises SR from 58.8 to 77.6 and lowers CR from 35.3 to 22.4. Conditioning the decoder on the map is not enough, because letting the map choose the final mode matters most: handing the choice back to the classification head collapses SR to 14.1. Refreshing only where things are (terrain and collision) on the current frame, while reusing the VLM's meanings, recovers the accuracy lost to VLM lag (single-frame variant: SR 65.9, CR 32.9).
method: VLM scene decomposition: Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, given the front view, instruction and goal, returns four judgments as labels, scores and object indices on a pivot frame.

Actionable Cost map: CLIPSeg grounds terrain labels into M^T (Gaussian-smoothed), and YOLO-World boxes punch graded Gaussian holes for M^C. M^H is a seven-zone heading score interpolated across columns, and M^P is a Gaussian corridor boost between passable object pairs. They compose as M_in = clamp(γ^-1 M^T ⊙ (1-M^C) ⊙ M^H ⊙ M^P).

Pivot–current design: all four components are baked on the pivot frame. Each current frame rebuilds only M^T and M^C by rerunning the segmenter and detector, with no new VLM call, giving a current map.

AC-Map-conditioned decoders: K=10 anchor-based regression or truncated-diffusion decoders attend over history, pivot-object, pivot-semantic and current-semantic streams (CLIP features + map encoder) plus a lag token e_N, trained with L1 + jerk + CE loss. The goal reaches them only through M^H.

AC-Map-scored mode selection: maps are projected onto a BEV grid, and each candidate is scored s = r_cur · r_pv · r_align. A safety veto zeroes any candidate with r_cur < τ and stops the robot if none passes.
Training-free variant: a metric-depth network (Depth Anything V2) lifts the maps to a world BEV cost grid, and sampling-based MPC over unicycle rollouts plans on it with no learned decoder.

setting.backbone: Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (frozen VLM) + CLIPSeg + YOLO-World (frozen) + trained regression / diffusion trajectory decoders with frozen CLIP ViT-B/16 encoder
setting.training_data: Decoders trained on SCAND, GND and a self-collected teleoperated Vision60 dataset, 20 epochs on one H200. The MPC variant is training-free.
setting.observation: egocentric front-view RGB with frame history and past poses (plus metric depth for the MPC variant)
setting.action_space: H=10 predicted waypoints at 0.5 s in the body frame, tracked by a low-level controller as velocity commands (v, ω)
setting.simulator: DynaNav benchmark (Spot quadruped replacing the wheeled robot); real-world Vision60
setting.privileged: none (point goal and language instruction given as task input)

numbers.eval_set_note: official 85-episode protocol (25 each hospital/office/warehouse, 10 outdoor), Spot quadruped

results: On DynaNav, RECAST reaches 80.0% SR (diffusion) and 77.6% SR (regression), against the strongest prior NavDP† at 66.7%, and the regression decoder gets the lowest CR at 22.4%. On a real Vision60 quadruped it gets 77.1% SR and 28.6% CR versus NoMaD's 45.7% and 42.9%. Even the training-free MPC variant (71.8% SR) beats all prior methods on SR.
limitations: Performance is bounded by the grounding models (CLIPSeg, YOLO-World): whatever they miss never enters the map.
The pivot–current design does not predict obstacle motion, so the gap between the stale pivot and the current frame remains for moving obstacles.
It relies on a slow proprietary VLM and hand-tuned score thresholds that differ between simulation and the real robot.
